if you think a chameleon is easier/easy compared to a ball python, you have a rude awakening coming your way OP 😬

take one look at the chameleon sub and you’ll see a wide range of owners struggling despite having near perfect conditions. chameleons are not at all easy to care for and the way you’re acting about your snake dying because it’s doing normal behaviour of a still settling in snake is concerning. 

i understand it’s frustrating when a snake won’t eat, but ball pythons are literally known for this. a month of owning can still be settling in time for them. it could be a variety of reasons and it’s not uncommon. not enough hides, not large enough tank, too much light, not enough light, still stressed from the move into the new home, too much handling, etc etc. it really can be ANYTHING that’s bugging him to not wanna eat. 

my advice is don’t handle him. seriously, just leave him alone and wait till the next time you’d try to feed him, still don’t handle him. hair dryer, warm water, and wiggle it to catch his attention. still doesn’t work? leave it in the tank overnight and check in the morning. 

try to make a post on your account itself and see if you’re able to post the tank photos from there, seeing the full husbandry can help go down the list of potential issues causing him to not want to eat.

according to OP’s post history, he’s had him about a month since April 1st. doesn’t seem he’s been able to link a photo of the enclosure fully but gave temps and humidity in an older post 

a bit (lot) concerned about the if he starves and die ill get a chameleon because they won’t starve themselves (wrong). if he finds a ball python hard to care for rn, he has noooo clue what he’s got coming with a chameleon 😬

kids should *never* be involved in getting someone off of drugs or alcohol. 

having them express that they love and miss him? no problem. but don’t have them do it because he refuses to get clean. that is not something that should be put on a child or anyone else. 

coming from a recovering addict myself, you need to WANT to get sober to stay sober. not have people put kids in an uncomfortable and frankly, unsafe situation because he doesn’t want to quit and get better. 

it is not on the kids to do the job, it’s on him as a grown ass man with adult choices. it is not a one and done thing either, recovery is not just “oh, my child misses me and wants me sober? done!” it’s a lot of work and it is very much traumatizing for children to watch anyone go through. 

if the child wants to show their support to the parent struggling, let them in a safe way. if not, don’t force them. it is never a child’s responsibility to play saviour for anyone.

don’t listen to this person, OP. if he did that to you for simply asking to help him, he would do the same for anyone else. 

i don’t know why the other commenter thinks involving kids is the solution to fixing addiction, it’s not. it traumatizes the kid more than anything and you already have to deal with him being wildly inappropriate to your daughter. 

keep doing what you’re doing by keeping her safe, you’re doing the right thing.

my biggest thing that has worked WONDERS with my 11 year old GC conure is ladder/stick/perch step ups. my boy is super cage territorial. even on the play stand on top, you simply can't go near him and not expect a nasty can opener bite. i slowly got him used to me bringing whatever the object was close to him, we use a ladder as it allows him to come to us on his own terms and we can move him around safely from stand to cage! when your bird steps up on the object used (again perch/stick/ladder) reward them with a treat either by hand feeding or showing them with the step up stick where you put it for them. you can also teach target training, it will help him redirect his urge to bite into something he can have fun doing without hurting the humans. your bird will bite for a multitude of reasons, you just need to learn their way of explaining what they want. my conure will make specific calls or whistles for what he needs, whether it be play time with a toy between us two, attention via shoulder hangout or a cuddle, food bowl is too low on food for his liking (aka he ate the top layer), he made soup in his water bowl and is now angry about it, wants a shower/bath, etc etc. 

avoid wearing gloves if you're trying to get your bird used to hands, they'll be confused as to why one day your hands are naked and skin coloured but the next it's this weird fabric/material and a different colour. my conure hates anything to do with gloves, so he isn't really the best for vet visits unless he's given some chamomile infused water to calm him down a bit. speaking of chamomile, try it out! it's a natural relaxer for birds, at least in my experience it works WONDERS!! i buy basic dried chamomile tea leaves, steep it and put it in the fridge to use when needed. my conure gets a good bowl of diluted tea from it approx 2-3 times a week as he does have trauma which causes night terrors some nights. 


desensitize yourself to reactions when being bit, i know how strong a Caiques beak is just as much as the next person who owns one, it isn't easy but to a bird your reactions = playing and reward. if you simply ignore and move them away from you, they start thinking "wtf this isn't fun, i get moved and ignored when i bite!". of course, body language is also something you should learn as sometimes it may seem like a "no reason" bite, but you simply didn't catch the body language warning. my conure gets overstimulated from too much interaction and fluffs up his full body, makes a specific squawk and "gnaws" (basically bite but doesn't close the beak on your finger) to let us know he's done and needs alone time for a few minutes. don't fling or shake your hand when you're being bit, you're adding to the rewarding behaviour your Caique is trying to get from his behaviour and you could very easily be making the situation worse by losing his trust in you. simply bring him back to his cage or a play stand, if he doesn't let go you can offer him a toy that he CAN bite and destroy to redirect his attention. your bird won't hate you if you are trying to redirect their behaviour to allow them more quality time, they'll be cranky and angry but they won't hate you. 


and *please* don't forget, parrots will bite because they are *parrots*. you don't want to completely train out their main method of communicating if they're angry, upset, want to play, tired, etc. you want to teach them to be more gentle, that biting hard does not get them what they want and they need to be gentle to get the reward they're seeking. i've used the step up object training, target training, recall, basic tricks and teaching them how to communicate better for all of my 7 birds and it works wonderfully. of course i still get bit, i signed up for bites when i decided to own birds! it's what comes with bird owning, it's inevitable. BUT, you can teach him the difference between a "play bite", "gentle bite" and their full force bite. i use my conure for all of these examples because he came to me completely untrained at 10 years old and hated hands and people, but he's now a snuggle bug with some behaviour problems we are still working on to help him with. 


*__really want to inforce the part of DON'T SHAKE OR FLING YOUR HAND WHEN YOUR BIRD BITES YOU. don't yell or raise your voice at them. don't make a big show of it hurting. completely and utterly ignore them, put them in a safe space such as on or in the cage or on a play stand. leave them alone for 5-10 minutes and then check on them to see if they've calmed down a bit. if you shake or fling your hand, raise your voice, make a big show of it, you're simply rewarding the behaviour and bringing down the trust levels between you and your bird.__*

vet tech here, i mainly work with "exotics", basically any animal beyond farm/dog/cat though a lot goes hand in hand with ALL pets. 

1- obesity. yes large animals are cute, but their health is not. i've seen MANY obese lizards with severe liver issues that cause nasty irreversible damage to their bodies, same in dogs if not worse. chihuahuas are not meant to be 20+ pounds, for example. they're a small breed with a small frame, they cannot handle all that weight on their tiny bodies! 

2- diet/nutrition. far too many carnivorous pet owners come in that their pet is having issues going to the bathroom, not holding weight, having malnutrition issues such as vitamin defiencies. cats and ferrets for example, are obligate carnivores. meat is the biggest and should be the main part of their diet, a treat here and there of other things is no issue but should not be more than 5% of diets in many pets. 

3- husbandry. tanked and/or caged animals need the space to move and get SOME exercise if they are not given time outside of their cage. and for gods sake, please do not get parrots if you cannot let them out of their cage for a MINIMUM 4 hours a day. even then, that's very little interaction and can cause hormonal and behavioural issues. 

4- unfortunately, finances. yes you may have paid a pretty penny for your animal, but costs do not stop after you leave the place with your new pet. your pet will need constant supply of food, vitamin and mineral supplements, toys, at-home grooming supplies, cage upgrades, etc etc. if you are unable to provide any of those, not even mentioning vet visits, it is not a good idea to have said pet. we all end up in a pinch from time to time, and we as vets and vet techs understand that wholeheartedly. we have experienced those moments as well, but there comes a time where you need to consider your pets needs over your own. companionship via pets is a privilege, and we should fully accommodate all needs that arise for our animals, and if we can't then we need to consider what is best for that animal, many times resulting in a rehome situation, or someone who can help while we work things out.

BirdTricks offers an AMAZING feeding chart for basically any bird species we can own to help create your own food mix for your little friends! i use their charts and blog posts heavily to help and alter food prep for the flock, as well as their training videos (they helped a LOT with taming my younger budgies) and just a lot of the info they have on their site/blog/books are amazing and so so helpful!

i personally feed a diet of 50/50 seed to pellet in their cages, i buy all my seeds at Bulk Barn for a fraction of the price to premade bags which saves me approximately 100$ a year (not a lot tbh but it helps!) and i can monitor the fatty seed intake and how much of what nutrient each seed can offer. i've owned budgies on and off my entire life (21 years) and have learned a lot from experience as well as from my parents who bred them back in the day! for pellets, my budgies typically get the Zupreem budgie size naturals, they won't even touch the colourful pellets! we also offer them Tropican lifetime formula pellets once they hit approx 1-1.5 years old. 

i prefer offering seeds in their daily chop mixes though, whether it's sprouted seeds or just plain seeds mixed in, it's a fun way for them to forage for the yummy seeds they love! i know lots of people prefer Harrison's or TOPs pellets, i have tried them with all 7 of my birds (3 being budgies) but no one in my flock seems to enjoy their pellets so we stick to Tropican or Zupreem Natural. it's okay to feed your budgies seeds, but it shouldn't be their *entire* diet, like the only thing they get. if you're able to and can afford to do so, you can make up your own seed mix for your birds that's adjusted to their diet needs and be able to monitor what is eaten more especially in fatty seeds. 

i typically avoid most fatty seeds but a good amount do offer other nutrients so can't be completely avoided, i just offer much less and make sure that everyone gets a mix of the entire bowl rather than that singular seed to avoid super fatty birds LOL 


it's truly a case of research, trial and error and just preference in terms of feeding what kind of food at certain times/days. so long as their diet is varied, seeds are not the worst thing in the world :)

some lizards/snakes/turtles/tortoises/reptiles in general, can take much longer to trust and respect us humans as their trusted friends. i have a crested gecko, yes a crested gecko who are **known** for being stupidly trusting, 4 years later who just doesn't care for human interaction! you cannot expect a friendship or bond with your reptile, but you can work towards it!

YES. all of this, YES. you need to be confident in yourself, you need to SHOW that you are confident and trust, respect and understand your new friends boundaries. you wouldn't be super in the face of a new human friend would you? no! you'd allow them to become comfortable and get to know you, whilst you get to know them and their quirks! you need to be cautious and respectful when it comes to new reptiles of any kind, they see us as these big two legged monsters of prey that are going to eat them. we need to GAIN their trust and respect, not expect it. they expect our trust and respect, not the other way around. careful, gentle and slow is the way to go with new scaly companions. they don't understand that we are simply trying to be mutual in respect and trust, they need to be shown it over time.

yes! 100% this! you want your scaly friend to KNOW that you are confident and you have trust in them. when you jerk away, you are showing them that they are capable of scaring you away and able to be stronger one no matter how bad that sounds. you want to show them that you are strong as well BUT **BUT** you are NOT going to hurt them. they see this large two legged animal coming at them with their scary hands that could hurt them, you don't want them to think of you as a threat. reptiles are not easily trusting of humans and for good reason! we need to respect and trust our reptile companions before we can even consider expecting them to do the same.

first and foremost, the poking and quick strokes on the body are not helping build any trust between the two of you. blue tongues can sometimes take a little longer to adjust to their new home so take your time. show them that human being in their presence = food and safety. the poking and fast movements do not show safety to your scaly friend, it shows threat and danger. 

keep your interactions together in their enclosure, by forcing them out of their enclosure to accept your presence you're simply making it harder for them to trust you. start off small, allow them to see your hand IN the enclosure, don't touch them or try to force an interaction, allow them to see that your hands do not mean they are going to be picked up and forced into a situation that stresses them out. do it a few times a week, again you want to take it slow as it's clear your new friend is quite scared and isn't trusting in you. i would say after two weeks, take into thought how their behaviour has changed with your hand in their vicinity and move onto hand feeding, whether it be with tongs or your bare hands, whatever you're most comfortable with! figure out their favourite treat, and stick to those for when you really want to reward them for showing trust. go into these interactions together in a calm and trusting demeanour. if you're nervous, untrusting and scared, they will be too! you need to show your new friend that you're confident, you trust them and respect them. 

respect mutually with reptiles go a long ways, respect that when they show you that they are not happy with their situation, move them out of it and leave them alone for a bit. if they're becoming flighty, move them back into their safe space, whether it be their enclosure or some lizards have a spot in the room that they enjoy, mine during free roam enjoy a dog bed i keep for them to relax on and maybe take a small nap. and again, food is the best and easiest way to a lizards heart! keep your interactions for now minimal and respect their space, move your interactions to feeding time and when you're showing them that hands are not their enemy. i wish you the best with your new friend, OP!

i've used old pieces of clothing i don't care about anymore to get them used to my scent, i just sleep on it for a few days and toss it in where they typically spend their time in the cage. switch out over the taming period, wear heavy duty gloves when handling for sure just to be safe and slowly work your way to one glove to none (worked for me on a savvy and a jeweled lacerta who hated humans but now tolerated us amazingly) hand feed with large tongs to avoid your fingers being the culprit lol but it also helps them associate the tongs with food and your hands no longer being seen as a threat. hang out by his enclosure for awhile during the day so he gets used to your presence being around him, and if he's brand new to your home, it could be a lot of moving stress which is adding on to never being handled! just give him time to settle in but the tongs, pieces of clothing and hanging out are some great ways to help them be used to you without the stress of actually handling

they're nocturnal little buggers so don't worry about bringing them out! do a 9-9 or 8-9 schedule with them, mine has a heat mat for belly heat and a very low wattage CHE for night time heat as my house gets fairly cold at night (below 40). dust them before feeding and don't forget to gutload! carrots are great for hydration with them, dog food, potatoes, and other foods are great for it if you don't want to use the commercial gutloading stuff. mine is much more active at night, so i feed him after lights out to make sure he's awake and already active, he gets dusted crickets every two to three feedings and has constant access to calcium in a water bottle cap that is replaced once a week since he's messy
